title: Perform primary meat inspection incisions of beef

lessons.title: Planning and preparing for beef inspection incisions
lessons.html:
Purpose of primary incisions

Primary meat inspection incisions are the routine cuts made into specific lymph nodes, muscles and organs of every bovine carcass to expose lesions that cannot be seen from the surface. They are prescribed by the regulations under the Meat Safety Act 40 of 2000. The aim is to detect conditions such as bovine measles, tuberculosis and liver fluke, while causing as little damage and contamination as possible.

Preparing the inspection point

  • The inspection station must have good lighting, so that colour changes and small lesions can be seen.
  • Head, pluck and viscera inspection points must be arranged so that the parts of each animal are presented together and can be matched to the carcass by number.
  • A hand-wash basin and knife sterilizer must be within reach, with the sterilizer at the correct temperature.
  • A detention rail and condemned containers must be close.

Equipment

  • At least two sharp inspection knives, so one is always in the sterilizer.
  • Steel for maintaining the edge.
  • Hook for holding and turning organs.
  • Detention tags and recording sheet.
  • PPE: clean protective clothing, hard hat or hairnet, boots, apron, and cut-resistant glove on the non-knife hand where policy requires.

Before slaughter begins

  1. Check the ante-mortem record for animals needing special attention.
  2. Check that the line is arranged to present head, tongue, pluck, liver, viscera and carcass correctly.
  3. Confirm communication with the line supervisor for stopping the line or moving carcasses to detention.

lessons.title: Performing the incisions on beef
lessons.html:
A fixed routine

Incisions are made in the same order on every carcass, as set out in the regulations and your training. A fixed routine prevents steps being missed. The main areas are listed below; follow the exact sequence and number of incisions you were trained in.

Head

  • Observe the head, mouth, lips and eyes.
  • Incise the main lymph nodes of the head, such as the mandibular (submaxillary), parotid and retropharyngeal lymph nodes, by slicing them so the cut surface can be seen. Look for enlargement, abscesses and caseous or calcified lesions that may indicate tuberculosis.
  • Incise the external and internal masseter (cheek) muscles with long, flat cuts parallel to the bone to look for measles cysts.
  • Observe and palpate the tongue.

Pluck

  • Observe and palpate the lungs; incise the bronchial and mediastinal lymph nodes.
  • Open the heart sac and examine the heart; incise the heart to expose the ventricles and septum, looking for measles cysts.
  • Observe and palpate the liver; incise the portal lymph nodes; incise the bile ducts to check for liver fluke.

Viscera and carcass

  • Observe the stomachs, intestines, spleen and mesenteric lymph nodes.
  • Observe the carcass inside and out: pleura, peritoneum, diaphragm, kidneys, and visible lymph nodes. Additional incisions are made where findings require.

Technique

  • Use clean, single, decisive cuts. Avoid hacking, which damages meat.
  • Sterilise the knife after each carcass and immediately after cutting into a lesion.
  • Do not let organs touch the floor or other carcasses.
  • If lesions are found, keep all parts identified and detain them.

lessons.title: Completing the primary inspection
lessons.html:
Linking findings

After the incisions, the findings from head, pluck, viscera and carcass are put together. A lesion in a head lymph node, for example, means the carcass and other organs must be examined more carefully for spread before a decision is made.

Actions at the end of inspection

  1. No abnormalities: the carcass and organs continue for marking as passed.
  2. Localised lesions: mark the parts for removal; ensure removal into condemned containers.
  3. Suspicious or serious findings: detain the carcass with its head and organs, tag them, and refer to the meat inspector or veterinarian.
  4. Suspected controlled disease: stop, detain, and report immediately, following the abattoir's emergency procedure and the Animal Diseases Act 35 of 1984.

Records

  • Carcass number, owner and findings.
  • Parts removed and reasons.
  • Detentions and referrals.

Cleaning up

  • Sterilise all knives and hooks.
  • Clean the inspection station during and after the shift.
  • Store knives safely and keep them sharp.

Common mistakes

MistakeConsequence
Skipping masseter incisions when busyMeasles missed; public health risk
Not sterilising after cutting an abscessContamination of the next carcass
Losing the link between head and carcassCorrect judgement impossible
Deep, ragged cutsLoss of meat value

Key points

  • Primary incisions are prescribed routine cuts that expose hidden lesions.
  • Prepare a well-lit station with sterilizer, two knives and detention facilities.
  • Follow the same sequence on every carcass: head, pluck, viscera, carcass.
  • Masseter and heart incisions target measles; lymph node incisions target tuberculosis and other infections.
  • Sterilise after every carcass and after cutting a lesion, and record all findings.
